title: Math Story Words
objectives: I can tell what total, difference, and remain tell me to do in a math story.
I can use half, double, twice, and each to talk about groups and parts.
I can make a close guess with estimate and check it.
I can write and say a short math story with a math word.
rationale: Second-grade math is full of story problems, and a few small words decide whether children add, subtract, or compare. The eight words split into finding a whole or what is left (total, remain), comparing and checking (difference, estimate), and parts and groups (half, double, twice, each). Children act out each story with objects before they write a number sentence, so the word meaning is clear. The unit uses than, both, guess, and detail from earlier units because these ideas show up again in every story problem.

words.def: All of the parts added together.
words.ex2: Add the coins to find the total.
words.nonExample: One part of the sum is not the total.
words.rel: finding the whole or what is left

apps.academic: Add the parts to find the total.
apps.spoken: What is the total of 6 and 7?
apps.writing: Write a number sentence with a plus sign to show the total.

cloze.s: Add 6 apples and 3 pears to find the ___ number of fruits.

cloze2.s: Tia counted all of her stickers, and the ___ was 12.

misuse.s: The total is what is left after you take some away.
misuse.why: A total is everything added together, not what is left after taking away.

visual.alt: A plus sign beside an apple.

words.def: How much one number is bigger than another.
words.ex2: Find the difference between my 12 stickers and your 7.
words.nonExample: Adding two numbers does not give the difference.

apps.academic: Subtract to find the difference between two numbers.
apps.spoken: What is the difference between 10 and 6?
apps.writing: Write a subtraction sentence to show the difference.

cloze.s: To find the ___ between 10 and 6, subtract: 10 minus 6.

cloze2.s: The ___ between her 15 marbles and his 9 marbles is 6.

misuse.s: The difference between 8 and 3 is 11, because you add them.
misuse.why: A difference is found by subtracting, and 11 is the total.

words.def: To make a close guess using what you know.
words.ex: Let us estimate how many beans fill the jar.
words.ex2: Pablo estimated that the rope was about ten steps long.
words.nonExample: Counting every item exactly is not estimating.

apps.academic: Estimate first, then count to check.
apps.spoken: I estimate that this is about 20.
apps.writing: Use about when you estimate: about 20 beans.

cloze.s: Before counting the crayons, ___ about how many are in the box.

cloze2.s: We can ___ the length of the desk by using our hands.

misuse.s: To estimate, count every item perfectly and write the exact number.
misuse.why: An estimate is a close guess, not an exact count.

words.def: To be left after some is taken away.
words.ex: Three cookies remain on the plate.
words.ex2: After the party, only two balloons remained.
words.nonExample: The part you take away is not what remains.
words.rel: finding the whole or what is left

apps.academic: Subtract to find how many remain.
apps.spoken: Two seats remain on the bus.
apps.writing: Write a subtraction sentence to show how many remain.

cloze.s: If you eat 3 of the 8 grapes, 5 will ___ on the plate.

cloze2.s: Eight kids were in line, and then three left, so five ___.

misuse.s: I ate all ten cookies, so ten cookies remain.
misuse.why: Remain means left after some are taken away, so none would remain.

words.def: One of two equal parts of something.
words.ex: Please give me half of the sandwich.
words.nonExample: A piece that is bigger than the other is not a half.

apps.spoken: I ate half of my apple.
apps.writing: Draw a line to split a shape into halves.

cloze.s: The pie was cut into two equal pieces, and each piece is one ___.

cloze2.s: I ate ___ of my apple and saved the rest for later.

misuse.s: Half of the pizza is a tiny slice, and the other piece is huge.
misuse.why: A half is one of two equal parts, so the pieces must be the same size.

visual.alt: A pizza and a division sign.

words.def: Two times as much or as many.
words.ex: Make a double batch of cookies for the party.
words.ex2: A double scoop of ice cream has two scoops.
words.nonExample: Half of a number is not its double.

apps.academic: Double a number by adding it to itself.
apps.writing: Write a sentence with double to tell about two times as many.

cloze.s: For a ___ batch, use two cups of flour instead of one.

cloze2.s: She ordered a ___ scoop of ice cream, so she got two scoops.

misuse.s: A double portion is half as big as a regular portion.
misuse.why: A double portion is two times as big, not half as big.

visual.alt: A peace sign beside an ice cream.

words.ex2: Our dog barked twice at the mail carrier.
words.nonExample: Doing something once is not twice.

apps.academic: Twice as many means two times as many.
apps.spoken: I brush my teeth twice a day.
apps.writing: Use twice to tell how many times something happens.

cloze.s: I washed my hands ___, once before lunch and once after.

cloze2.s: Mom said she would call us ___ today, in the morning and at night.

misuse.s: I clapped my hands twice, and I only clapped once.
misuse.why: Twice means two times, so one clap is not twice.

visual.alt: Clapping hands next to a peace sign for two.

words.def: Every one of a group, one at a time.
words.ex2: Put two crackers on each plate.

apps.academic: There are 3 groups with 4 in each group.
apps.spoken: Each of us has a turn.
apps.writing: Use each when the same amount goes with every one.

cloze.s: There are 4 bags, and ___ bag holds 3 apples.

cloze2.s: The teacher walked around the room and gave ___ student a new book.

misuse.s: Each student has a book, so only one student has a book.
misuse.why: Each means every one in the group, so every student has a book.

visual.alt: A basket and an apple to show one apple in each basket.

passage.title: Lena's Stickers
paras: Lena had 12 stickers. She gave each of her 3 friends 2 stickers. The total she gave away was 6, and 6 stickers remain.
Half of her stickers are gone. The difference between 12 and 6 is 6. Her brother estimated that he had double her 6, so he counted twice to check.

qs.q: In the story, the total Lena gave away was
qs.why: She gave 2 stickers to each of 3 friends, so the total was 6.

qs.q: How many stickers remain with Lena?
How many stickers does her brother have?
qs.why: He has double her 6, which is 12.

write.prompt: Write a short math story. Use total or remain.

study.task: Pick one math story word and act it out with counters or crayons. Draw your picture and write a number sentence. Tell a partner your story using the word.

groups.label: finding the whole or what is left

sentences: Write a math story that uses the word total.
Write a sentence about something you can cut in half.
Write a sentence about something you do twice a day.

combine.model: Mia and Leo have a total of 8 pens.
Five grapes remain after Ben ate four.

discuss: How is a total different from a difference?
When is it a good idea to estimate, and when should you count exactly?
produce.explain: Explain how double and twice are alike. Give one example with numbers.

argue.prompt: Which is easier to find, a total or a difference? Pick one and give a reason.
argue.frame: I think finding a ___ is easier because ___.

constructed.prompt: Write a math story that uses total and remain.
look: tells a question or an answer
constructed.model: Mia had 8 pencils and Leo had 4. The total was 12. She gave away 5, so 7 remain.

constructed.prompt: Tell about a number. Say half of it and double it.
look: names the number in the answer
constructed.model: The number is 8. Half of 8 is 4. Double 8 is 16.

teacher.overview: Children learn eight words that appear in math story problems and use them to act out and write math stories. Use counters and bar drawings. Check each word with a real action: add for total, take away for remain, and compare for difference. Revisit than, both, guess, and detail in each story.

notes.va.total.n: Total means all together. Use two groups of counters and push them together. Children often think total always means add large numbers; link it to an action. Spanish: total.
notes.va.difference.n: Difference here is a math word: how much more or less. It also means not the same, as in different. Use two bars of cubes and match them. Spanish: diferencia.
notes.va.estimate.v: An estimate is a close guess using something you know, such as a benchmark. Estimating is not wild guessing; ask what helped. Always check afterward.
notes.va.remain.v: Remain means what is left. Use take-away stories with counters. The related word remainder appears in later grades. Spanish: quedar or sobrar.
notes.va.half.n: Half is one of two equal parts. Fold paper to show equal parts. Children often call any piece a half; check that parts are the same size.
notes.va.double.adj: Double means two times as many. Use doubles facts: 4 and 4. Children may confuse double with half; do both in one picture.
notes.va.twice.adv: Twice is two times. Use it with actions: clap twice. Link to double: twice as many is double.
notes.va.each.pron: Each tells about every one in a group. Use equal groups, such as 3 plates with 2 crackers each. Pair with the idea of fair sharing.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The story says there are 4 bags and each bag has 3 apples. Each tells me every bag has 3. I will draw 4 bags with 3 apples in each. The total is 12, and I can check by adding 3 four times.'
discuss: Which math story word tells you to take away?
How can an estimate help you check an answer?
misconceptions: Children may think difference always means subtract without thinking; ask what is being compared.
Some children think half is any part. Half needs two equal parts.
Children may confuse twice and double as the same. They are alike in number, and double can be a describing word.
extend: Write a class math story book where each page uses one word.
Estimate how many objects are in a jar, then count them to check.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit than, both, guess, and detail: compare two numbers with than, tell what is true for both groups, guess before counting, and add a detail to the story.

wida.oral: Say a short math story with a partner. Use one of the eight words and let your partner act it out with counters.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (total, diferencia, estimar, quedar, mitad, doble, dos veces, cada) not reviewed by a native speaker; quedar and sobrar both work for remain.
Check the math in the passage: 12 - 6 = 6; 3 friends x 2 = 6; double 6 = 12.
